background.definition: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rare bacterial infection of the deeper layers of skin characterized by widespread necrosis of the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and superficial fascia easily spreading across the fascial plane. Fournier's gangrene is a type of NF of the perineal and perianal regions that also often involves the genital regions of both men and women; it can rapidly spread along the fascial lines and involve the retroperitoneum.

list.listitem: 0.4 to 0.53 cases per 100,000 population per year.

A systematic review of 27 studies found that monomicrobial infections mostly affected the extremities, while polymicrobial infections were associated with Fournier gangrene. Staphylococcus aureus, bacteroides spp, and streptococcus pyogenes were the most common pathogens.

Based on data from a systematic review of 11 studies with 355 patients, the microbiology of NF of the extremities is as follows: Staphylococcus aureus (19%) Streptococcus group A (14%) Streptococcus viridans (10%) Staphylococcus coagulase negative (9%) Staphylococcus other species (9%) Escherichia coli (7%) Coryneform bacteria (6%) Pseudomonas species (5%) Clostridia species (5%) Enterobacter species (5%) Vibrio species (5%) Klebsiella species (4%)

Type I infections are polymicrobial and are more common. An average of five pathogens are typically cultured from Type I infections, comprised mainly of bowel or genitourinary flora. Type II infections are monomicrobial, most commonly caused by S. pyogenes, and carry higher mortality.

Diabetes, smoking, IV drug use and alcohol abuse are common comorbidities.
A large case series found an association with obesity.
It is a rare complication of bullous pemphigoid (0.4 to 15 cases/100,000).
Pathogens enter through skin portal and have rapid growth; the secretion of harmful toxins stimulates cytokine release.
Cytokines damage endothelial lining, which leads to fluid leaking into the extravascular space causing diminished blood flow, tissue hypoxemia, and tissue death.
Adjacent tissues experience vasculitis and thrombosis, and further necrosis occurs involving subcutaneous nerves.
Toxins leaking into the bloodstream can lead to bacteremia (up to 60%), sepsis, and possible death.

Suspect necrotizing fasciitis (NF) when a patient presents with cellulitis and pain out of proportion to the severity of the lesion, signs of systemic toxicity (hypotension, tachycardia, and hyperthermia), bullae, patches of cutaneous necrosis, or tissue crepitus. B

If above are negative but clinical presentation is still suspicious for NF, order blood cultures, CBC, serum sodium, hemoglobin, glucose, serum creatinine, and albumin,
and consider imaging (CT, MRI) or in children, ultrasound or MRI. B

Differential.Differential_Features: No crepitus on PE, no systemic signs of toxicity other than possible fever
Raised advancing borders and sharp edges due to lymphedema
Use LE Doppler to identify clot
Often painless and without positive culture
Exfoliative skin disease caused by toxin-producing strains of Staphylococcus aureus

list.listitem: Ask about pain, fever, shortness of breath, and preceding trauma.

Suspect necrotizing fasciitis (NF) in patients with cellulitis and pain out of proportion to the severity of the lesion, signs of systemic toxicity (hypotension, tachycardia, and hyperthermia), hemorrhagic bullae, patches of cutaneous necrosis, or tissue crepitus.
See for frequency of symptoms in patients presenting with NF.

If NF is clinically suspected, order CBC, blood cultures, serum sodium, hemoglobin, glucose, serum creatinine, and albumin.
This information can be used to calculate the LRINEC score (below). Consider CT or MRI imaging if the diagnosis remains in doubt (or in children, ultrasound, or MRI).
In a series of 451 patients with NF of the upper and lower limb, 13% had gas on x-ray, 7% soft tissue swelling on x-ray, 7% albumin <3.0 g/dL, and only 2% hyponatremia.
WBC greater than 15.4 x 109/L and sodium less than 135 mEq/L provide strong evidence in favor of NF. If both are normal, the diagnosis is very unlikely.

X-rays can be more sensitive than physical exam for the detection of soft-tissue gas, with radiographic findings present before crepitus is detected. However early findings of NF can appear similar to cellulits on radiography.
MRI with gadolinium has been reported to accurately show fascial inflammation and detect fascial necrosis. If no deep fascial involvement is revealed then NF can be excluded.

CT is the primary imaging modality in the work up of NF given availablitiy and high spatial resolution. Gas within fluid collections along subfascial planes are the hallmark findings of NF. Other findings may include asymmetrical fascial thickening, subcutaneous emphysema, fluid accumulations, and abscess formation. CT can also help with treatment planning by showing whether or not the infection has spread up the fascial plane to the perineal structures or the retroperitoneum as well as identifying the potential infectious source.

Positive ultrasound findings include an echolgenic layer of gas above the deep fascia with posterior acoustic shadowing, distorted thickened fascia often times with fluid accumulation, and diffuse fascial thickening.

In a systematic review (n=221 patients), point of care ultrasound had an overal overall sensitivity ranging from 85.4% to 100% while the specificity ranged from 44.7% to 98.2%. Fluid accumulation along the fascial plane was the most sensitive (85.4%; 95% CI 72.2%-93.9%), while subcutaneous emphysema was the most specific (100%; 95% CI 92.5% - 100%).

Transcutaneous tissue oxygen saturation measuring using near infrared spectroscopy, a noninvasive reliable method for assessing patients, has shown to be extremely accurate for identifying and diagnosing NF when O2 saturation falls below 70%. Ultrasound can also detect soft tissue air.
Findings at surgical exploration and skin biopsy are the only absolute means of diagnosis.

The laboratory risk indicator for necrotizing fasciitis (LRINEC) is a simple model that has been developed and validated to distinguish NF from nonnecrotizing skin infection using only objective laboratory findings (see ).

Integrating MRI findings (including thickening of deep fascia ≥3mm and multi-compartmental involvement) with the LRINEC score has been shown to improve positive (82% vs 79%) and negative predictive values (77% vs 67%) compared to the LRINEC alone (see ). A score ≥5.5 corresponds to 50% probability of NF.
See for a suggested approach to management.

Give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately when high clinical suspicion is present with coverage for both aerobes, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, and anaereobes (ie, a carbapenem such as meropenem 1 g every 8 hours or a beta-lactamese inhibitor ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5 to 3.0 g every 6 to 8 hours or piperacillin-tazobactam 3.37 g every 6 to 8 hours plus vancomycin 15mg/kg every 12 hours or linezolid 600mg IV every 12 hours, all given IV). B
Urgent surgical exploration, debridement, and fasciotomies are critical. C
Fluid replacement and nutritional support improves outcomes. B
Consider amputation if no viable tissue left or with infection that is unable to be controlled with other treatments. C

Give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately when high clinical suspicion is present. IDSA guidelines recommend ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5 to 3.0 g every 6 to 8 hours or piperacillin-tazobactam 3.37 g every 6 to 8 hours plus clindamycin 600 to 900 mg/kg every 8 hours plus ciprofloxacin 400 mg every 12 hours for suspected mixed infection, all given IV. Alternatives include imipenem/cilastatin 1 g every 6 to 8 hours IV; meropenem 1 g every 8 hours IV; ertapenem 1 g once daily; or cefotaxime 2 g every 6 hours plus either metronidazole 500 mg every 6 hours IV or clindamycin 600 to 900 mg/kg every 8 hours IV.
For patients with severe penicillin hypersensitivity, use clindamycin or metronidazole with an aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone.

After etiology is confirmed, begin direct antibiotic treatment toward the specific organism guided by sensitivities. For Streptococcus infection, penicillin 2 to 4 MU every 4 to 6 hours IV plus clindamycin 600 to 900 mg/kg every 8 hours IV are recommended. For S. aureus infection, nafcillin, oxacillin, cefazolin, and vancomycin (if resistant) are recommended.

A Cochrane review evaluating interventions for necrotizing soft tissue infections in adults found scarce evidence for medical therapies such as antibiotics and adjuvant treatments like intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and CD28 receptor antagonists. Evidence was deemed very low quality due to a paucity of trials, small sample sizes, and many studies with high risk of bias.
Topical silver sulfadiazine has shown good efficacy following debridement of necrotic tissue.
Urgent surgical exploration, debridement, and fasciotomies are critical for survival. Repeat surgical debridement is necessary in most cases (mean number 3 per patient).
Skin and muscle grafting have shown success, and decreased healing time after infection has cleared.
Amputation if no viable tissue left or with infection that is unable to be controlled with other treatments.
A Cochrane review evaluating interventions for necrotizing soft tissue infections in adults found scarce evidence for surgical therapies.

A systematic review of studies comparing skin-sparing debridement with en bloc debridement found only 9 case series and a single cohort study. The authors were unable to conclude whether skin-spring debridement was non-inferior to more extensive procedures.
IV immunoglobulin has sporadically been reported to reduce mortality.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is the standard treatment for clostridial myonecrosis; however, it has been proposed as an adjunct to other treatment modalities to inhibit growth and kill anaerobic bacteria. It is reported to be most helpful before end organ damage occurs. However, a Cochrane review evaluating adjunctive HBOT for necrotizing fasciitis did not find randomized trials evaluating its efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness.

Vacuum-assisted closure (VAC; KCI, San Antonio, Texas) delivers negative pressure therapy that has been reported to be effective in managing wounds and decreasing morbidity associated with nonhealing open wounds.

A systematic review of VAC identified 7 trials with 249 participants. Compared with a conventional dressing, patients the VAC groups had lower mortality (OR 0.27, 95% CI 0.09-0.87) and a trend toward shorter hospital stays (mean difference -8.5 days, 95% CI +0.5 to -17.5). Complication rates and the number of debridements needed did not differ between groups.
Nutritional support is often necessary secondary to insensible losses.
Immediate hospitalization and surgical referral when high degree of suspicion is present.

Hypotension on presentation, delay in surgery more than 24 hours, temperature <37 degrees Celsius, infection of the head/neck/thorax/abdomen, infection with vibrio Aeromonas, cirrhosis, soft tissue air, older age, renal dysfunction, elevated aPTT and the band form of NF are associated with increased mortality, while hemorrhagic bullae are associated with decreased mortality. B
WBC more than 15.4 x 109/L, sodium less than 135 mEq/L, and elevated interleukin-1 receptor antagonist are associated with increased mortality and hypoalbuminemia. B

A clinical decision rule was developed to predict mortality in patients with necrotizing fasciitis, and found that age over 60 years, dependence prior to hospitalization, dialysis, emergency operation, pre-operative septic shock, and decreased platelet count were independent predictors of mortality. B
Histopathologic findings of few to no PMNs and positive Gram stain have a significantly increased rate of mortality and poorer prognosis. B

Rate of limb loss was 22.3% in one series, and overall mortality rate ranges from 23% to 76%. Two large case series with a range of necrotizing acute soft tissue infections found 8% to 13% mortality rate. B
In children, the most common etiology was group A Streptococcus following infection with varicella.
These cases have decreased following the introduction of the varicella vaccine.

cell.label: Cellulitis with associated pain out of proportion to the severity of the lesion, signs of systemic toxicity (hypotension, tachycardia, and hyperthermia), bullae, patches of cutaneous necrosis, or tissue crepitus?
Continued high clinical suspicion for NF in patients with edema of the limb, induration, purulence, or fluctuance?
Treat cellulitis. If it worsens recalculate LRINEC score, measure transcutaneous O2 saturation, and consider imaging.

Order CBC, chemistries, and CRP and calculate LRINEC score (). Consider transcutaneous oxygen saturation, if available. Consider imaging (CT, MRI or ultrasound) if diagnostic uncertainty. Is LRINEC = 6, oxygen saturation <70%, and/or imaging suggestive of NF?

Emergent surgical referral to evaluate for NF. May need imaging (ie, MRI, CT, ultrasound, radiographs) to determine depth of involvement. Empirically start broad-spectrum antibiotics (eg, ampicillin/gentamicin/ clindamycin), IV fluids, and nutritional support.
